Jarāsandha
(‘one [whose body was] joined by Jarā’)
------------------------------------------
Jarāsandha was the powerful monarch of the kingdom of Magadha and a contemporary of कृष्ण and the Pāṇḍavas. His capital was Girivraja.
Bṛhadratha, his ड़थेर्, had no issues for a long time. Once, at his request, a sage, Caṇḍakauśika by name, gave him a mango sanctified by a मन्त्र and asked him to give it to his wife. Since Bṛhadratha had two wives, he cut the fruit into two halves and gave a piece to each of them. Each gave birth to half a baby. Alarmed at this grotesque turn, the two queens threw away the ‘babies’. Jarā, an ogress who was searching for ड़ोओद्, found the pieces and joined them when they became a baby-boy. She took it to the king Bṛhadratha who suitably rewarded her. Since the boy was ‘joined’ (sandha or sandhāna) by the lady Jarā, he came to be known as ‘Jarāsandha’.
After जरासन्ध became a strong young man, capable of taking over the kingdom, Bṛhadratha crowned him and left for the forest to live as a vānaprasthin (forest-recluse).
Jarāsandha’s daughters had been married to कṁस. Since कṁस was killed by कृष्ण, जरासन्ध became his bitter enemy. His several invasions of मथुरा (the capital of कृष्ण) and attempts at killing him proved infructuous.
Being a worshipper of भैरव (a terrible aspect of शिव), जरासन्ध had imprisoned a large number of princes from other kingdoms with a view to sacrificing them to his deity. When कृष्ण got wind of the news, he managed to get him killed in a duel with भीम, the second of the Pāṇḍava princes and put his son सहदेव on the throne.

Jaratkāru
------------------------------------------
A sage in the lineage of the great ṛṣi भृगु, जरत्कारु got this name because he had made his body old and dilapidated due to excessive austerities (Jaratkāru = made old).
Once he found that his ancestors were in a miserable state due to the lack of obsequial rites, normally performed by the descendants. He then decided to marry and beget children. He married a girl, whose name also was जरत्कारु, and who was the sister of the serpent king वासुकि.
His son out of this union was Āstīka, the sage who successfully stopped the सर्पयाग or the serpent sacrifice being conducted by जनमेजय, the son of परीक्षित्, to avenge his ड़थेर्’s death at the hands of the serpent तक्षक.
